# Harrison-McCabe test for heteroscedasticity

<small>Source: [`R/performHarrisonMcCabeTest.R`](https://github.com/DiogoRibeiro7/heteroTests/blob/main/R/performHarrisonMcCabeTest.R) · Help: `?performHarrisonMcCabeTest`</small>

Orders the observations by a variable and tests whether the share of the
residual sum of squares that falls in the first part of the ordered sample
is too small, or too large, for errors of constant variance. The p-value is
exact under normal errors, given the regressors.

## Usage

```r
performHarrisonMcCabeTest(
  model,
  data = NULL,
  order_by,
  point = 0.5,
  alternative = c("less", "two.sided", "greater")
)
```

## Arguments

`model`
:   A fitted [stats::lm](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/lm.html) object, with or without weights, or a
    [stats::glm](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/glm.html) with the Gaussian family and the identity link.

`data`
:   The data frame `model` was fitted to, or `NULL`, the default. The
    residuals, design and weights are read from the fit itself, and so, since
    0.16.0, is its rank, decided at the tolerance of the fit (see the section
    on the rank), where the test decided the rank of the design again at
    `1e-7`; `order_by` is read from the rows of `data` that hold the
    observations of the fit. Without `data` it is read from the model frame of
    `model`, which holds it only when it is a variable of the model under its
    own name (`x`, not `log(x)`); a model that transforms the variable it is
    ordered by needs `data`, as does an ordering variable the model does not
    use. Since 0.16.0, data that are given are matched to the observations of
    the fit: rows with row names of their own by name, in any order; rows that
    only number themselves (a tibble, a data.table, a data frame whose row
    names were reset) by the row numbers of the fit, or in the order of the fit
    when they hold one row per observation. The rows the fit dropped may be
    there or not. Data whose rows cannot be shown to hold the observations of
    the fit are refused; see [`test_results`](test_results.md).

`order_by`
:   Character scalar naming the column of `data` that orders the
    observations. Tied values keep the order the observations have in the
    fitted model.

`point`
:   The size of the first part of the ordered sample. A number
    strictly between 0 and 1 is a fraction of the sample, and the first part
    then holds `floor(point * n)` observations, as in [`lmtest::hmctest()`](https://rdrr.io/cran/lmtest/man/hmctest.html). A
    whole number of 1 or more is the number of observations. Each part must
    hold at least as many observations as the model has coefficients.

`alternative`
:   Character scalar. `"less"` (the default) is the
    alternative that the variance increases with `order_by`, which makes the
    share small; `"greater"` that it decreases; `"two.sided"` either. The
    two-sided p-value is twice the smaller of the two one-sided ones, capped
    at 1, as in [`performGQTest()`](performGQTest.md) and in the default of
    `skedastic::harrison_mccabe()`.

## Value

An object of class `htest` with the share `HMC` as the
statistic, the number of observations in the first part `m` and the sample
size `n` as parameters, the p-value, and the alternative in words.

## Details

With \(\hat{e}_{(1)}, \dots, \hat{e}_{(n)}\) the
least-squares residuals in the order of `order_by`, the statistic of
Harrison and McCabe (1979) is

\[
b = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{m} \hat{e}_{(i)}^2}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat{e}_{(i)}^2},
\]

the share of the residual sum of squares that falls in the first \(m\)
observations. A variance that increases along the ordering makes \(b\)
small, and one that decreases makes it large. It is the statistic of
[`lmtest::hmctest()`](https://rdrr.io/cran/lmtest/man/hmctest.html).

The 1979 article was not consulted for this implementation. The definition
follows Harrison (1981), by its first author, which restates the statistic
with \(m\) the integer part of \(n / 2\) and rejects for small
\(b\), and it agrees with [`lmtest::hmctest()`](https://rdrr.io/cran/lmtest/man/hmctest.html).

Under normal errors of constant variance, \(b\) is a ratio of quadratic
forms in normal variables, and its distribution depends on the regressors.
With \(M\) the residual-maker of the design in the ordered sample and
\(D\) the diagonal matrix that selects the first \(m\) observations,

\[
P(b \le b_0) = P\left(\sum_j (\lambda_j - b_0) z_j^2 \le 0\right),
\]

where the \(z_j\) are independent standard normal and the
\(\lambda_j\) are the \(n - k\) eigenvalues of \(M D M\) on the
residual space, \(k\) being the number of coefficients. They are found
from the \(k\) singular values of the first \(m\) rows of an
orthonormal basis of the design, and the probability is evaluated by
Imhof's (1961) formula with [`stats::integrate()`](https://rdrr.io/r/stats/integrate.html), as Harrison (1981) does
for the exact variant of the test. For a constant and a linear trend, the
5% critical values this gives at 10, 20, 30 and 40 observations are those
of Harrison's (1981) Table 3 to the three decimals printed there. Under the
null hypothesis the mean of \(b\) is
\((m - \sum_{i \le m} h_{(i)}) / (n - k)\),
with \(h_{(i)}\) the leverages in the ordered sample.

The probability is computed to an absolute accuracy of about `2e-11`.
Smaller p-values are not resolved, and a statistic far in a tail can return
a p-value of 0.

The p-value depends only on the space spanned by the regressors, so it does
not change with the parametrisation of the model.

## The rank

\(k\) is the rank of the fit, the number of its coefficients that are
not aliased, decided at the tolerance the fit used: `1e-7` for an `lm`, or
the `tol` it was given, and `1e-11` for a `glm` (since 0.16.0). Before, the
rank was decided again at `1e-7`, so a Gaussian `glm`, or an `lm` fitted
with a smaller `tol`, whose design holds a column that is a combination of
the others to within `1e-7` but not to within its own tolerance, was given
a null distribution of a smaller rank than its residuals. With
`x3 = x1 + 1e-9 * rnorm(120)` the `glm` has rank 4, and its p-value is
0.002273 where it was 0.002288, computed with rank 3. On every other fit
the two ranks agree and the value is unchanged.

## Direction of the alternative

In [`performGQTest()`](performGQTest.md) and [`performSzroeterTest()`](performSzroeterTest.md) the statistic grows when
the variance increases along the ordering, and in this test it shrinks. The
alternative names the tail of each statistic, so the same hypothesis, a
variance that increases with `order_by`, is `alternative = "less"` here and
`alternative = "greater"` in those two functions. In all three it is the
default, and the `alternative` element of the result states it in words.

## Weighted fits

On a fit with weights the statistic is computed from the Pearson residuals
\(\sqrt{w_i}\, \hat{e}_i\), and the null distribution from
the weighted design \(\sqrt{w_i}\, x_i\). Both are those of
the equivalent unweighted regression, so the test asks whether the weights
are adequate. The weights of a Gaussian `glm` are its prior weights.

## Heavy tails

The null distribution assumes normal errors. In the designs of
`inst/validation/harrison-mccabe-size-power.R` the test rejects a true null
hypothesis 11.7% to 16.3% of the time at the 5% level when the errors
follow a \(t_5\) distribution, and more often the larger the sample;
[`performGQTest()`](performGQTest.md) and [`performSzroeterTest()`](performSzroeterTest.md) do the same. When the tails
may be heavy, use [`performGlejserTest()`](performGlejserTest.md) with the ordering variable as
`variable` and `robust = TRUE`, which in the same study rejects 4.7% to
4.9% of the time under those errors. Its default transformation takes the
absolute value of the variable, which preserves the ordering only when the
variable is positive.

## Reference implementations

The statistic agrees with [`lmtest::hmctest()`](https://rdrr.io/cran/lmtest/man/hmctest.html) to `1e-8`. Its p-value
does not: with `simulate.p = TRUE` it is simulated from residuals of a
regression on a constant alone, whatever the model, and with
`simulate.p = FALSE` it is `NA`. `skedastic::harrison_mccabe()` reports a
different p-value as well; `inst/validation/README.md` says why.

## Supported models

It accepts an `lm` and, since 0.16.0, a `glm` with the Gaussian family and the
identity link, unweighted or with positive weights, a `fitWLS()` fit and, since
0.16.0, a rank-deficient fit, which it tests on the estimable part of its
design: it gives the value of the same model fitted without the aliased columns.
The Gaussian `glm` with prior weights `w` is the least-squares fit
`lm(..., weights = w)`: it has the same design, residuals and weights, and it
states the normal errors of constant variance, given the weights, under which
the null distribution above is exact, so the test gives the value of the `lm`
when the two decide the rank alike (see the section on the rank). It refused
every `glm` before 0.16.0. It refuses a `glm` of another family or link, a
`survey::svyglm()` fit, a fit with a zero weight, a coefficient that is not
finite for another reason, and `data` that lack rows or variables of the fit.
It refuses a multivariate `lm` ("needs a model with one response"), since
0.16.0; before, it stopped with a coercion error. An `mgcv::gam()` fit is
tested as before 0.16.0, with smooth terms too, until a later step settles
which tests take such a fit; since 0.16.0 its observations are matched to the
rows of `data` by the row names of its model frame. Before, they were matched
by position, since the residuals of a `gam` carry no names, and `data` with
the rows of the fit in another order gave a wrong value. Which model each test
accepts, and why, is set out in [`test_results`](test_results.md), under *Supported models*.

exact variants of two tests for heteroscedasticity based on ordinary least
squares residuals. *The Economic and Social Review, 12*(4), 235–252.

Harrison, M. J., & McCabe, B. P. M. (1979). A test for heteroscedasticity
based on ordinary least squares residuals. *Journal of the American
Statistical Association, 74*(366a), 494–499.
[doi:10.1080/01621459.1979.10482544](https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1979.10482544)

Imhof, J. P. (1961). Computing the distribution of quadratic forms in
normal variables. *Biometrika, 48*(3-4), 419–426.
[doi:10.1093/biomet/48.3-4.419](https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/48.3-4.419)

## See also

[`performGQTest()`](performGQTest.md) and [`performSzroeterTest()`](performSzroeterTest.md) for the other tests along an
ordering of the observations; [`performGlejserTest()`](performGlejserTest.md) when the errors may be
heavy-tailed.

## Examples

```r
data(mtcars)
mod <- lm(mpg ~ wt + qsec, data = mtcars)
performHarrisonMcCabeTest(mod, mtcars, order_by = "wt")

# Variance that increases with x
set.seed(7)
x <- runif(80, 1, 5)
d <- data.frame(x = x, y = 1 + 2 * x + rnorm(80, sd = exp(0.3 * x)))
performHarrisonMcCabeTest(lm(y ~ x, data = d), d, order_by = "x")

# Either direction, with a third of the sample in the first part
performHarrisonMcCabeTest(lm(y ~ x, data = d), d,
  order_by = "x",
  point = 1 / 3, alternative = "two.sided"
)
```
